results.content: The global EV trade is facing rising barriers. The EU imposed 17%-38% tariffs on Chinese EV imports. Mexico has removed EV import tax exemptions for countries without free trade agreements. Canada and Turkey also imposed protectionist policies. In this context, we argue that, to meet EV penetration targets, partnering with Chinese companies to build local supply chains can be a feasible strategy for these countries. The affordability advantage of Chinese EVs can be largely maintained with [...] direct competition without tariff protection. Additionally, U.S.-based suppliers, such as Goodyear, Lear, and Qualcomm, produce parts for automakers in China, Japan, and the EU. Tariff escalation risks retaliation and complicates their international operations. [...] This situation is not unique. EVs from Japan, Korea, and the EU also face tariffs exceeding 25%, further reducing the affordability of EV products in the U.S. This means that the U.S. has to rely on the affordability of domestically produced EVs to incentivize consumer purchases, whereas EV sales suggest this strategy has not been successful. Moreover, the up-to-$7500 tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which primarily benefit U.S.-made EVs, are set to expire in September 2025.
